papers.abstract: We consider the Hill, Lane and Sudderth urn, in which a black or white ball is added at each step with probabilities depending on the current proportion of black balls. We solve the equation for the limiting normalized cumulant generating function when the urn function is invertible on the outer branches beyond the fixed points and the corresponding inverses are Lipschitz. The solution has a parametric representation through three quadratures of the urn function and a limit of compositions of radicals, with no derivatives or inverses of the urn function in the final formula. We prove an error bound that does not accumulate along the partition and remains valid when starting from the initial singularity. Four examples with exact solutions illustrate the two orientations of the construction, the non-affine case and the presence of zeros.
authors: Simone Franchini

papers.title: Subsystem evolution in the history state formalism
papers.abstract: We present a relational framework for characterizing the evolution of quantum composite systems, based on the correlations within a history state describing the whole evolution relative to a quantum reference clock. While total system-clock entanglement entropy consistently measures the unitary evolution of the closed global system, a different picture emerges for the reduced state of an open subsystem, whose evolution is generally non-unitary due to environmental coupling. We introduce a general formalism that quantifies open-subsystem dynamics using a subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state. We demonstrate that this quantity serves as a consistent quantifier of subsystem evolution with respect to a given clock basis, can be applied to arbitrary dynamics, and reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit. Furthermore, maximizing this measure over all clock bases yields a basis-independent bound on the maximum evolution achievable relative to the clock, directly linked to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Finally, we derive analytical expressions for qubit clocks, illustrate our results using spin 1/2 and spin 1 quantum walks, and present a full matrix formalism of Kraus operators for describing the most general subsystem evolution.
authors: A. Boette, F. Lomoc, N. Canosa, R. Rossignoli

papers.title: QWeaver: Quantum Circuit Cut Workflow with MLIR-based Compiler, Runtime, and Weaver Hybrid Tasks
papers.abstract: Quantum computers available today are constrained by limited qubit counts and high noise levels, making the direct execution of large quantum circuits infeasible on a single device, and while quantum circuit cutting addresses this by partitioning a large circuit into smaller subcircuits for independent execution, orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge. In this paper, we present QWeaver, a task-graph-based programming and orchestration workflow framework for quantum circuit cutting that accepts OpenQASM quantum circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. In this graph, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)-based circuit cut is the first task, responsible for analyzing and partitioning the input circuit into executable fragment representations; the generated fragments are then handed to a set of quantum circuit execution tasks that depend on the cut task and can be dispatched concurrently across available quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). Finally, a weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing that applies quasi-probability reconstruction techniques to combine the sampled measurement outcomes of all fragments and recover an accurate approximation of the original circuit's output distribution. We describe the architecture of QWeaver, its integration with Q-IRIS and the execution engine for the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR-EE), validate end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluate systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.
authors: Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Sharmin Afrose, Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble

papers.title: Spectral Engineering of Charge Localization and Work Reliability in Collective Quantum Batteries
papers.abstract: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on how much energy it stores, but also on how rapidly useful charge can be restored after work extraction. We show how engineering the reservoir spectrum connects these properties in an interacting collective-spin battery. Interactions separate the Dicke transition frequencies, allowing frequency-selective pumping and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the ladder. Analytical results relate the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Two reservoirs producing the same mean charge can nevertheless exhibit markedly different localization and charging times. Under repeated extraction, finite-time recharging also generates correlations between successive work outputs. At matched mean work, these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle and long-time fluctuations: a protocol with larger fluctuations in individual strokes can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, while relaxation modes distinguish recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Finally, local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, leading to an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction under a collective transverse controller.
authors: He-Guang Xu, G. D. de Moraes Neto

papers.title: Finite-time stochastic resetting in bounded domains: competing targets, energetic cost, and optimal search strategies
papers.abstract: We investigate the first-passage dynamics and energetic cost of a Brownian particle subject to finite-time stochastic resetting in a bounded one-dimensional domain with two absorbing boundaries. Unlike conventional instantaneous resetting, the particle is returned to a prescribed resetting position through a finite-duration process driven by a linear trapping potential. By solving the corresponding backward equations, we derive analytical expressions for the mean global first-passage time and the splitting probabilities. Our results show that the finite duration of the return process can substantially modify the dependence of the mean global first-passage time on the resetting rate. In particular, we identify a critical trapping strength above which resetting can accelerate the search process, and characterize how the range of favorable resetting positions depends on the trapping strength. We further characterize the energetic cost of resetting by deriving the generating function of the total work and obtaining an analytical expression for its mean value. For the linear trapping potential considered here, we establish an exact relation between the mean total work and the mean cumulative return time. This relation allows us to establish a quantitative trade-off between the mean global first-passage time and the energetic expenditure, revealing how the finite duration of the return process affects search efficiency. Brownian dynamics simulations confirm our theoretical predictions.
authors: Hanshuang Chen, Chongyao Tang, Guofeng Li

papers.title: Critical--localized reentry under periodic spacer control
papers.abstract: Tracking a fixed fraction of a quasiperiodic spectrum tests whether repeated critical--localized alternation extends over a nonzero spectral weight. We find such alternation in a matched-dimer chain by varying only the spacer on-site energies and following a fixed interval of integrated-density-of-states (IDS) labels. An exact Bloch-determinant identity links the physical transfer discriminant to the bands of a periodic reference operator. For the golden cell frequency, we prove that, on a common full-measure set of phases and for every finite value of the spacer control, the physical spectrum in the open reference bands is critical, with purely singular-continuous spectrum and zero Lyapunov exponent, while the spectrum strictly outside the bands is pure point, with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions. Validated IDS bounds certify repeated critical--localized alternation of the same fixed spectral fraction at successive spacer controls. Spacer shifts move the physical levels and reference-band edges at different rates, allowing us to reshape finite-chain return windows and place their endpoints at prescribed controls. An affine recalibration relocates the control family exactly.
authors: Xin Wang, Pei-Jie Chang, Dong Ruan, Gui-Lu Long

papers.title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory of Process Memory and Measurement Records
papers.abstract: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.
authors: Hai Wang

papers.title: From Powers--Stormer to Loewner Inertia: Weighted Trace Functionals and Orthogonal Perturbations
papers.abstract: We study the weighted trace functional $\TT_{f,h}(A,B)=\Tr h^\circ(A-B)[f(A)-f(B)]$, where $h^\circ(H)=h(H_+)-h(H_-)$. The Jordan decomposition of $A-B$ yields exact common-roof decompositions for operator monotone and operator convex functions, including the Powers--St\o rmer and Ricard trace comparisons. The orthogonal cross term gives a finite rank-one realization of the classical conditional L\"owner-matrix criterion for operator convexity. For powers, resolvent squares yield a coupling-dependent Mellin strip, endpoint identities, and quantitative bounds on off-sector spectral interactions. Linearization produces positive and inverse moment subspaces of power L\"owner matrices. A confluent determinant calculation provides the remaining sign data in the known inertia classification. We give explicit equality conditions and a finite-copy application of the Powers--St\o rmer equality case.
authors: Trung Hoa Dinh, Cong Trinh Le, Minh Toan Ho

papers.title: Covering the Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and the Design Effect of a Measurement Setting
papers.abstract: Quantum state tomography and shadow-based estimation rely on measuring Pauli observables. An experiment does not measure them one at a time: it chooses a measurement setting that assigns one of the bases X, Y or Z to each qubit, and a single run in that setting yields estimates of every Pauli observable compatible with it. We say that the setting covers those observables. We determine how many random settings cover a prescribed fraction of all Pauli observables. As the number of settings grows exponentially with the number of qubits, the covered fraction has a sharp threshold at a growth rate of $3^{3/4}$ per qubit, set by the rate-distortion function of covering at zero distortion. We give an explicit expression for the number of settings needed to reach a target fraction, accurate up to a remainder that reduces to a small oscillation for many qubits, and show that random sampling is asymptotically optimal up to a factor of less than 1.69. Coverage does not determine what a setting contributes to an estimator. Observables covered by one setting are estimated from the same outcomes, so their estimates are correlated. We quantify this correlation through the design effect of a setting, which equals the squared Pauli expectation that the setting captures and depends on the target state. We derive its mean over settings in closed form for every state and show that it can be estimated without bias from the measurement data. In simulations on six qubits, measuring settings needs 7.6 to 38 times fewer circuit runs than measuring the same number of observables independently. At high coverage, fitting the outcome histograms instead of averaged estimates roughly halves the reconstruction error, mainly because the fit counts how many settings cover each observable. The correlation itself costs such a fit about a factor of two, and a larger design effect signals more to gain from modeling it.
authors: Kausthubh Chandramouli, Noah Siekierski, Bojko N. Bakalov, Dror Baron

papers.title: Aharonov-Bohm blockade of complete reversal in coupled Rabi cavities
papers.abstract: When a common bias reverses two bistable fields, the system can pass through either of two single-reversal configurations on its way to the favored state. We show that interference between these two orders of reversal can block the final step. In a dimer of coupled quantum Rabi cavities, the four field configurations form a loop, and a complex photon-hopping amplitude threads it with an Aharonov-Bohm flux. Near half a flux quantum, the two paths to complete reversal interfere destructively: in microscopic simulations, a slow uniform sweep reverses one field with probability 0.998, although the final bias favors reversing both. A four-state model calibrated at zero bias predicts how the window of this Aharonov-Bohm blockade narrows with sweep time. The blocked state remains coherent. A differential pulse followed by a return sweep converts the relative phase of the two single-reversal configurations into a fringe in the joint field signs, with contrast 0.95. In a trimer, a phase gradient imprinted between sweeps determines whether the next sweep adds or removes a reversed field: reversing the second of two gradients changes the most probable outcome from three reversed fields to one.
authors: Shu He, Liwei Duan

papers.title: Comparing Data-Driven and Numerical Weather Prediction Forecasts of Extreme Weather: A Review
papers.abstract: Data-driven weather forecasting models, chiefly trained on reanalysis data, now match or beat physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) models on most headline scores, but whether this advantage extends to extreme weather is contested. We review peer-reviewed studies that directly compare data-driven forecasts with NWP for extremes, from nowcasting to subseasonal lead times. We discuss grey literature in the outlook but do not include it in the formal review. There is good agreement on the fact that data-driven models mostly outperform NWP on temperature extremes, tropical cyclone tracks and the location of synoptic features across time scales. The evidence is mixed for extreme precipitation and feature-based extreme event detection such as extremes related to atmospheric rivers, while it leans toward better NWP performance for estimating event intensity. For record-breaking events that lie outside the training distribution, the evidence is narrower. Nonetheless, both a systematic global evaluation and several case studies find that physics-based models retain the advantage, with data-driven models underestimating both the frequency and the magnitude of records. Hybrid systems that post-process NWP with machine-learning (ML), or couple data-driven forecasts with physics-based models, deliver some of the largest and most consistent gains. We argue that headline scores, verification choices and case selection explain much of the apparent disagreement in the literature, and provide recommendations for a more trustworthy and interpretable evaluation of data-driven models for extreme and record-breaking weather.
authors: Gabriele Messori, Hiu-Wang Lau, Chenyu Dong, Gianmarco Mengaldo, Leonardo Olivetti

papers.title: Localized active phase in the coevolving voter model with fixed links
papers.abstract: The coevolving voter model (CVM) describes the evolution of node states and network topology through copying and rewiring dynamics. It traditionally assumes that all ties can be rewired, overlooking unbreakable real-world relationships like family or close friendships. To address this, we introduce fixed links that cannot be rewired and study how these structural constraints modify the collective dynamics of the CVM. In addition to the active and frozen phases of the CVM, we find a new localized active phase in which activity is sustained, beyond a percolation transition, by a giant component of fixed links. The existence of this new phase is predicted by a moment-closure approximation that goes beyond the standard pair approximation. The finite-size manifestation of this phase is an asymmetric fragmented phase. In addition, the active-frozen transition of the CVM, manifested as a fragmentation transition for finite systems, is delayed by the existence of fixed links to larger values of the rewiring rate.
authors: Hoseung Jang, Maxi San Miguel, Byungjoon Min

papers.title: Imaging chiral snake states in a qubit array with programmable gauge fields
papers.abstract: Spatially varying magnetic fields steer charged particles along directed paths. Where a field reverses sign, particles follow snake-like orbits along the reversal line, in a direction set by both the field orientation and the sign of their energy. Transport measurements have detected such snake states, but imaging their dynamics in a reprogrammable field landscape remains challenging. Here we digitally simulate the Harper--Hofstadter model with programmable synthetic magnetic fields on a 49-qubit superconducting processor. In each Trotter step, every hopping term is one native fractional-iSWAP gate, and single-qubit $Z$ rotations set all 36 plaquette fluxes independently, without additional entangling gates. Uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes reveal Aharonov--Bohm suppression of diagonal propagation, disorder-induced slowing, and magnetic reflection. At a field reversal, bonding and antibonding initial states, which carry opposite energy biases, propagate in opposite directions, and both directions reverse when the field is inverted. A symmetry analysis of these reversals yields a chiral displacement of nearly one lattice spacing after ten Trotter rounds, with symmetry-breaking residuals below 0.05 lattice spacings. Bond-resolved flux programming with site-resolved imaging thus provides a quantitative tool for synthetic gauge fields and a route to time-dependent gauge fields and interacting particles.
authors: Hanyi Wang, Lijun Sun, Bihao Guo, Weizhi Tao, Jian Ding, Shengbin Wang, Xinfang Zhang, Wei-Yong Zhang, Hantao Sun

papers.title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
papers.abstract: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$ logical qubits, where $\epsilon$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$.
authors: Christopher A. Pattison, Jeongwan Haah, John Preskill

papers.title: A structure-based model of the bacterial chemosensory array reveals how the scaffolding protein CheW tunes sensory responses
papers.abstract: We introduce a structure-based Ising model of the bacterial chemosensory array to investigate how the scaffolding protein CheW tunes signaling responses. The model couples the activity states of core signaling units and of CheW subunits within hexameric rings on a lattice with the structure observed in cryoEM experiments. Recent experiments show that increasing CheW participation in hexameric rings raises response cooperativity in non-adapting cells and sensitivity in adaptation-proficient cells. Our lattice model quantitatively reproduces both effects, while mean-field theory shows that CheW increases the effective coupling between core units, sharpening the response in both cell types. The statistics of CheW placement (complete hexameric rings versus random distribution) substantially alter how responses vary with CheW abundance. Moreover, different coupling strengths can yield the same static response yet markedly different activity fluctuations and dynamics. CheW abundance further controls a crossover from relaxational to oscillatory fluctuations, whose location depends on the spatial distribution of CheW. These dynamical signatures, including oscillations predicted near native CheW levels, are testable by single-cell dynamics measurements. Combined with CheW titration and our modeling results, these measurements can probe the array's assembly dynamics and allosteric couplings. Beyond the chemosensory array, our approach can generalize to other large protein complexes, providing a framework to study the functional role of scaffolding proteins and allosteric interfaces in signal processing.
authors: David Hathcock, Yingxin Zheng, Yuhai Tu

papers.title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
papers.abstract: Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.
authors: Louis Follet, Paavai Pari, Isidor Schoch, Thien Nguyen, Justin G. Lietz, Daniel Lowell, Brucek Khailany, Krysta M. Svore, Dirk R. Englund, Taylor L. Patti

papers.title: Analysis of the Second-Harmonic Generation Process in Nonlinear Metasurfaces Based on Multiple Quantum Wells: The Approach of Nonlinear Current Density, and The Development of Boundary Conditions
papers.abstract: Using plasmonic metasurfaces integrated with nonlinear materials, such as multiple quantum wells (MQWs), has been an excellent solution to enhance nonlinear light-matter interactions. In this approach, a plasmonic resonator enhances the intensity of the fundamental harmonic within the MQWs region, increasing the strength of the intersubband transitions inside the MQWs. As a result, the efficiency of second harmonic generation (SHG) increases significantly. In this paper, we present a new approach to analyze the SHG process in nonlinear metasurfaces based on MQWs. In this approach, first, we formulate the nonlinear current density within the MQW region, which serves as the radiation source of the second harmonic wave. Notably, the saturation effect in MQWs, that limits the nonlinear response, is accounted for. Second, we address the development of boundary conditions for the second harmonic (SH) field in periodic structures, which ultimately leads us to define periodic boundary conditions for the SH field. Third, we combine these elements into a semi-analytical framework and validate it against previously reported experimental data. Finally, an efficient MQWs structure and plasmonic metasurface are designed for the fundamental wavelength of 8 $\mu$m. After implementing the proposed algorithm, we observe that the designed nonlinear metasurface achieves a significant conversion efficiency of 0.02% under the incident intensity of 23.5 kW/cm$^2$. KEYWORDS: Second harmonic generation, metasurface, multiple quantum wells, nonlinear current density, periodic boundary conditions
authors: Sepehrdad Bahrami

papers.title: Faster than square-root run-time in adiabatic quantum algorithms for Exact Cover 3
papers.abstract: By intertwining ideas from sequential and adiabatic quantum computing, we propose a quantum algorithm for the problem class Exact Cover 3, which is a sub-class of 3-satisfiability (3-SAT) problems and NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) complete. We find a quantum run-time which is significantly faster than the square-root run-time $N\to N^{1/2}$ of the Grover algorithm. Depending on the structure of the problem (e.g., connectivity of clauses), the run-time scaling may range from approximately third root $N\to N^{1/3}$ to nearly fourth root $N\to N^{1/4}$, possibly even faster.
authors: Gernot Schaller, Ralf Sch\"utzhold

papers.title: Spectrum of the parity operator for parafermions and parabosons from character formulas
papers.abstract: In a recent paper [J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. 59 175201 (2026)] Green's triple relations for parafermions and parabosons were extended by including a new operator $P$, referred to as the parity operator. The spectrum of $P$ in Fock space representations was computed, making use of the action of parafermion (resp.\ paraboson) creation and annihilation operators. In the current paper, we adopt a different method to compute the spectrum of $P$, namely using character formulas. For a set of $n$ parafermions, the action of $P$ is deduced from character formulas of $so(2n+2)$. For a set of $n$ parabosons, the known spectrum of $P$ yields new character formulas of particular $osp(2|2n)$ representations.
authors: N. I. Stoilova, J. Van der Jeugt

papers.title: Blanket theory for dense networks
papers.abstract: We show how Blanket theory provides a constructive method for calculating cavity functionals in dense spin networks. Building on the description through interfaces and magnetization shells, we develop the calculation from the low-temperature fluctuations around the ground state. In this regime, dilute defects reveal the mechanism of random energy model (REM) universality for linear energies, while their sharing and renewal across layers organize the energies and Gibbs weights into a hierarchy. Because the same configurations determine the covariances of the fresh cavity fields, this construction identifies the fields and weights with an Aizenman-Sims-Starr random overlap structure. The cavity contributions can then be evaluated through recursive fractional means, yielding an explicit free-energy functional parametrized by layer magnetizations and hierarchical exponents, with coefficients determined by the interaction variances and the network normalization. Under the stated moment and normalization conditions, comparison of pressures transfers the limiting mean pressure from the Gaussian representative to networks with independent centered non-Gaussian couplings having the same variances. We illustrate the method with the deterministic Curie-Weiss model, recover the Parisi functional for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, and derive the functionals for restricted and deep Boltzmann machines, including the full replica symmetry breaking (fullRSB) limit.
authors: Simone Franchini

papers.title: The $S$ and Double-Exponential Transformations with a Moment Expansion for Three-Centre Coulomb and Hybrid Integrals
papers.abstract: Three-centre two-electron Coulomb and hybrid integrals over exponential-type functions involve semi-infinite radial integrals containing oscillatory spherical Bessel functions. We investigate the combination of the $S$ transformation with Fourier-type double-exponential (DE) quadrature for their accurate and efficient numerical evaluation. The $S$ transformation transfers derivatives from the spherical-Bessel factor to the radial amplitude, converting the integral into a sine representation particularly well suited to Fourier-type DE quadrature. Numerical comparisons demonstrate that the combined $S+\mathrm{DE}$ approach can substantially reduce the number of quadrature nodes required to achieve high accuracy compared with direct DE. We further identify a geometry-dependent oscillation-to-damping ratio and establish a convergent moment expansion in the weakly oscillatory regime. Exploiting this complementary representation markedly enhances the numerical reliability of the algorithm in regimes where direct oscillatory quadrature becomes inefficient. The method is examined through semi-infinite radial integrals and complete H$_2$O and C$_2$H$_4$ molecular integrals over Slater-type functions, with comparisons against complete $S$-series evaluations and values reported in the literature.
authors: Hassan Safouhi

papers.title: Analysis of a Homodyne-Like Measurement Scheme Using Photon Counters and Weak Local Oscillator
papers.abstract: In standard homodyne detection, an unknown optical signal state is combined with a local oscillator (LO) at a beam splitter (BS), and the appropriately integrated intensities at the two outputs of the BS are subtracted to obtain an approximate quadrature measurement. Accurate quadrature measurements require a high-amplitude LO and high-efficiency detectors. By varying the LO phase, the optical state in the mode matching the LO can be reconstructed. In many practical settings, a high-intensity LO is not desirable, which has led to the exploration of homodyne-like measurement schemes that replace photodiodes with photon-counting detectors and use an LO with a low average photon number. In this paper, we investigate what features of the unknown state can be determined by counting the total-photon number in one or both outgoing paths after the BS, keeping the mode of the LO fixed but adjusting its phase and magnitude. We find that it is possible to determine the unknown optical state in the mode matching the LO conditional on the number of photons in the orthogonal modes on the same path. If both the phase and the intensity of the LO can be varied, the statistics of just one of the detectors is sufficient to infer these parameters, but both detectors are required when the LO has a fixed intensity. Our analysis is carried out in the infinite-data limit, assuming access to the full photon-number distribution from one or both detectors.
authors: Arik Avagyan, Emanuel Knill, Scott Glancy

papers.title: Quantum Mpemba effect in a driven-dissipative atom-waveguide coupled system
papers.abstract: The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) describes the counterintuitive phenomenon in which a more strongly perturbed quantum system relaxes toward its steady state faster than a less perturbed one. Here, we investigate the QME in a weakly driven-dissipative atomic array coupled to a one-dimensional chiral waveguide. Starting from the steady state, we introduce a local quench by resetting a single atom to its ground state and examine the subsequent relaxation dynamics. We find that quenching atoms near the array boundaries induces faster initial relaxation through enhanced coupling to superradiant modes and direct photon emission into the waveguide, giving rise to an edge-enhanced QME. Strong directional decay further amplifies this effect by promoting the spatial accumulation of superradiant modes near the preferred boundary, leading to a skin-enhanced QME. At later times, relaxation is increasingly governed by long-lived subradiant modes localized predominantly in the bulk of the array. By coupling two atomic arrays with different interparticle spacings, we further demonstrate an interface-induced QME, where quenching an atom near the interface makes the system relax more slowly at early times but approach its steady state faster at later times, owing to weak participation in both superradiant and subradiant modes. Our findings reveal how the spatial structure of collective decay modes and directional dissipation jointly govern anomalous quantum relaxation, offering potential routes toward accelerated steady-state preparation in waveguide QED systems.
authors: Hao-Kai Chi, H. H. Jen

papers.title: Efficient Spectra and Dynamics with Tangent-Space Chebyshev Tree Tensor Networks
papers.abstract: We present a tangent-space Chebyshev method (TaChe), which combines tree tensor network states with Chebyshev recursion and maximum entropy spectral analysis in a tree tensor network tangent space, for quantum many-body spectra and dynamics. Implemented tensor network state calculations in the tangent space of the ground state, the core advantage of TaChe is that it can substantially reduce the computational complexity, memory usage, and numerical instability associated with tensor network state compression. Implemented on the GPU platform, it produces accurate spectra with speedups of up to $46.8$ over the previous Chebyshev tensor network method and $13.7$ over one-site time-dependent variational principle propagation in the reported benchmarks. Applications to acetonitrile, thermal aggregate emission, finite-temperature charge transport on a \(6\times6\) lattice, and internal conversion in aggregates of up to 100 molecules demonstrate the efficiency and versatility of TaChe in simulating complex molecular systems.
authors: Zhangyu Yang, Xingyao Wu, Shuo Sun, Yu Wang, Weitang Li, Jan von Delft, Christian B. Mendl, Zhigang Shuai

papers.title: Geoneutrinos (and reactor neutrinos) do not visibly decay
papers.abstract:
Neutrinos that decay on their way to a detector arrive depleted, more so at low energies, where time dilation lengthens their lifetime the least. Geoneutrinos---electron antineutrinos from the radioactive decay of uranium and thorium inside the Earth---have energies of a few MeV and travel up to the diameter of the Earth. We use them to test neutrino decay for the first time. We compute the geoneutrino signal at Borexino, KamLAND, SNO+, and JUNO for visible decay, in which the daughter neutrinos are themselves detected, and compare it against their published data. We find no evidence of decay that holds across Earth models. Combining the four experiments, we limit the decay $
u_1 	o 
u_3$ in the inverted mass ordering at 90% C.L.: $	au_1/m_1 > 3.7 	imes 10^{-9}$ s eV$^{-1}$ when the radiogenic power of the Earth is left free and $	au_1/m_1 > 4.4 	imes 10^{-9}$ to $1.6 	imes 10^{-8}$ s eV$^{-1}$ when it is taken from Earth models. With an Earth model assumed, the geoneutrinos set the limit; with the power free, the antineutrinos from nuclear reactors that the same experiments detect count as much as the geoneutrinos. These are the first terrestrial limits on the visible decay of $
u_1$.
authors: Mauricio Bustamante

papers.title: Free energy distribution for two non-crossing directed polymers on the cylinder
papers.abstract: We consider the partition sum $Z_L(t)$ of two non-crossing continuum directed polymers of length $t$, in a common random medium with the geometry of a cylinder of circumference length $L$. In the limit $t \to +\infty$, the $k$-th cumulant of (minus) the free energy $\log Z_L(t)$, grows as $c_k(L) t$, and we compute the amplitudes $c_k(L)$. To this aim we first study the integer moments $\langle Z_L(t)^n \rangle$, whose long-time behavior is determined by the ground-state energy of the one-dimensional attractive Lieb--Liniger model in the symmetry sector associated with the Young diagram $(n,n)$ (a two-component bosonic nested Bethe ansatz). This ground state energy is obtained using the nested Bethe-Ansatz involving $2n$ physical rapidities and $n$ auxiliary rapidities. The analytic continuation in the replica number $n$, which yields the cumulants $c_k(L)$, is performed through a non-trivial generalization of the method developed by Brunet and Derrida for a single polymer on the cylinder. We obtain fully explicit formulas for the mean $c_1(L)$ and the variance $c_2(L)$, and construct a systematic scheme for computing all higher cumulants $c_k(L)$. Finally, taking $L\to+\infty$ and $n\to0$ with $nL^{1/2}$ fixed, we derive a universal scaling function which characterizes the large-deviation statistics of the two-polymer free energy and is expected to be universal within the one-dimensional two-layer periodic SHE/KPZ class. The two tails of the large-deviation function are obtained analytically, revealing different roles of the non-crossing constraint in favorable and unfavorable fluctuations of the common disorder.
authors: Andrea De Luca, Pierre Le Doussal

papers.title: Positivity, Noise, and Cones
papers.abstract: As a consequence of causality, Euclidean-time correlation functions in quantum field theory are subject to constraints in the form of positivity conditions on certain Hankel matrices. Such conditions define convex conic structures. Correlation functions computed numerically using Monte Carlo techniques generally contain statistical fluctuations that violate the positivity conditions. This work describes a projection procedure, based on the convex conic geometry induced by the positivity conditions and a statistical covariance matrix, that can be used to restore positivity, providing a unique decomposition for noisy correlators into causal and acausal components. In contrast to previous literature, this work explicitly leverages the conic structure and not just the convex nature of the causal space. The projection can be computed using primal-dual interior-point methods. Constrained projection gives rise to observable-specific frequentist confidence intervals for smeared spectral densities in the causal bootstrap of [Phys. Rev. D 114, 074510 (2026)]. Analytic results are supported with numerical examples.
authors: Ryan Abbott, Claire X. Davis, Sarah Fields, William I. Jay, Patrick Oare, Matteo Saccardi

papers.title: Topological Origin of Directional Amplification in Arbitrary-Dimensional Non-Hermitian Lattices
papers.abstract: In non-Hermitian lattices, combinations of gain, loss and nonreciprocal couplings can generate exponentially growing directional amplification with applications in signal processing and precision measurement. An intriguing question is whether such amplification has a universal topological origin in arbitrary dimensions. Here we establish a dimension-independent framework to uncover the topological origin of directional amplification based on the concept of amoeba, which is the logarithmic image of the singularities of the response generating function. The complement of the amoeba in the logarithmic parameter space consists of connected components, each carrying a distinct and discrete topological label. We show that the asymptotic response is governed by the component extending toward negative infinity. When the origin of the logarithmic parameter space is outside this component and not on its boundary, there must exist some directions in which the response is exponentially amplified. Otherwise, there is no directional amplification in any direction. Our results provide a general topological criterion for classifying the responses in arbitrary-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices.
authors: Zhenxiang Wu, Linfeng Zhang, Haitan Xu

papers.title: A Lie-Group Approach to Alfv\'enic Turbulence: The SO(3) Rotational p-model
papers.abstract: The inner heliosphere is permeated by fully developed, highly intermittent nonlinear turbulence. Conventional stochastic models synthesize these multiscale fluctuations by injecting additive noise within a flat Euclidean space. However, such approaches fundamentally violate the topological constraints of ideal magnetohydrodynamics, inadvertently breaking the kinetic incompressibility of the plasma and introducing spurious magnetic compressibility. To preserve the exact geometrical invariants of Alfv\'enic fluctuations, a novel mathematical framework is presented: the rotational p-model. By mapping a multifractal singular measure directly into the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and integrating the associated stochastic differential equations in the Stratonovich sense on the spherical manifold $S^{2}$, the model generates highly intermittent, scale-dependent rotational dynamics. This Lie-group formulation conserves the magnetic field modulus while perfectly reproducing the fractional spectral envelopes and the non-Gaussian directional intermittency observed in space plasmas. Furthermore, by isolating purely directional reorientations, the framework provides exact analytical control over the waiting time statistics of magnetic intermittent bursts and the multifractal scaling exponents of angular deflections, offering a powerful new paradigm for the study of nonlinear turbulent phenomena.
authors: Daniele Telloni, Sabrina Guastavino, Gary P. Zank, Luca Sorriso-Valvo, Michele Piana

papers.title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
papers.abstract: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.
authors: Zhi-Lei Zhang, Lianxiang Cui, C. P. Sun, Kohei Nakajima, Kazuyuki Aihara

papers.title: Geometric Decomposition of Entropy Production Based on General $f$-Divergences
papers.abstract: We construct a general class of excess--housekeeping decompositions of entropy production based on $f$-divergences for overdamped Langevin systems. The excess entropy production rate equals the relaxation rate of the $f$-divergence toward a relaxation target and also admits an optimal-transport representation, while the housekeeping velocity preserves the same relaxation target. Our framework recovers the Hatano--Sasa and Maes--Neto{\v{c}}n{\'y} decompositions as special cases, and unifies their relaxational and optimal-transport aspects within a common structure. Moreover, our framework yields physically meaningful decompositions beyond these two by taking a desired distribution as the relaxation target.
authors: Rihito Nagase, Shoki Sugimoto, Takahiro Sagawa

papers.title: Distinguishing Conserved Quantum Sectors via Measurement Record Features
papers.abstract: Conservation laws partition the Hilbert space of a quantum system into invariant sectors that are often difficult to identify directly. Repeated measurements on an ancillary probe, however, generate a measurement record that provides information about the occupied sector. Here we develop a framework for identifying conserved sectors using a $(K+1)$-dimensional feature vector of record statistics, comprising the average outcome frequency and pair-outcome correlations up to $K$ measurement cycles apart. For fixed $K$, the feature vector can be evaluated at a cost linear in record length. In quantum non-demolition measurement models, the average outcome frequency suffices for accurate sector identification. For an interacting spin bath with nontrivial dynamics within each sector, incorporating temporal correlations between successive and more widely separated measurements into the record feature vector substantially improves classification fidelity. Our framework provides an efficient approach to conserved-sector identification and demonstrates the importance of temporal correlations in distinguishing the underlying sector dynamics.
authors: Hao Zhu, Guo-Feng Zhang, Wen-Long Ma

papers.title: Vanilla Adiabatic Quantum Optimization Can Have Subexponential Advantage
papers.abstract: We construct a family of objective functions $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ for which vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization along $H(s) = -(1-s)\sum_{i=1}^n X_i + s\sum_x f(x)\lvert x\rangle\!\langle x\rvert$ finds the global minimizer in $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time, whereas any classical algorithm requires $\exp(n^{\Omega(1)})$ time to do so in the black-box model. Our result is achieved by replacing the linearization technique in an earlier work of Leng et al. (arXiv:2504.14841), which establishes a similar subexponential quantum speedup using a transverse field Ising mixer rather than $-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$.
authors: Yufan Zheng

papers.title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States
papers.abstract: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance $d=9$ and on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.
authors: Jiale Huang, Yaojian Chen, Ke Liu, Dingshun Lv, Mingpu Qin

papers.title: Odd-Even Effects on Liouvillian Spectra and Relaxation Dynamics in Boundary-Driven Spin Chains
papers.abstract: We investigate odd-even effects on Liouvillian spectra and relaxation dynamics in boundary-driven XY and cluster chains. With the bulk couplings and boundary dissipation rule fixed, the parity of chain length determines whether non-decaying oscillatory modes exist. Consequently, odd- and even-sized chains exhibit qualitatively different dynamical behaviors. We trace this mechanism to the coupling between bulk Majorana paths and the boundary jump operators. An isolated path supports undamped modes, and products of an even number of its Majorana operators span a non?decaying subspace of even operators. This structure yields nonzero purely imaginary eigenvalues of the Liouvillian and persistent contributions to bond correlations or magnetization after preparation in product states. The mechanism extends to cluster interactions of even range under a fixed boundary dissipation rule. The existence and frequencies of the persistent modes are independent of the magnitudes of the positive boundary dissipation rates. Our results unveil how chain parity controls the existence of persistent dynamics.
authors: Zhen-Yu Zheng, Shu Chen

papers.title: Reliability of quantum communication over erasure channels
papers.abstract: Quantum information can be reliably transmitted at rates below the quantum capacity with an error that vanishes as the number of channel uses grows. The reliability function characterizes the optimal exponential decay rate of this error. For quantum erasure channels with a prime input dimension, we determine the reliability function exactly at all positive communication rates below capacity that meet or exceed an explicit critical rate. Notably, stabilizer coding strategies attain this optimal reliability throughout this regime.
authors: Hongyu Mao, Kun Fang

papers.title: CCZ gate beyond the strong Rydberg-blockade regime
papers.abstract: We present a protocol for implementing a controlled-controlled-Z (CCZ) gate on a neutral-atom platform, employing three individually addressable atoms confined in a linear array of optical tweezers and operating under finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction (RRI). The protocol combines successive excitation of the Rydberg atoms with analytically determined pulses and uses two Rydberg levels to access opposite-sign interaction shifts. We show two different paths to get the conditional phase in the target atom: a pair of target pulses with opposite phases and a single detuned target pulse followed by a local phase correction. We derive analytical expressions for the time-integrated Rydberg populations to calculate the associated decay errors and also evaluate gate performance through master-equation simulations. Numerical comparisons with a fast Rydberg-antiblockade (RAB)-based CCZ protocol show improved gate performance at larger interatomic separations within the parameter regime considered. Monte Carlo sampling further quantifies the sensitivity to thermally induced position fluctuations. These results identify the tradeoffs between gate duration, Rydberg-state exposure, and interaction sensitivity, providing an analytically specified route to native three-qubit phase gates beyond the strong-blockade regime.
authors: Snigdhadev Ray, Sinchan Snigdha Rej

papers.title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters
papers.abstract: Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.
authors: Mojtaba Asadollahi, Danial Khajehzadeh, Abolfazl Ramezanpour

papers.title: Stabilizer models of achiral abelian topological orders
papers.abstract: We construct continuous-variable stabilizer codes realizing every achiral 2D abelian topological order, both bosonic and fermionic. Starting from an arbitrary signature-zero integer $K$-matrix, we show that the corresponding topological order can be obtained by condensing a lattice of dyons with trivial pairwise mutual braiding in an $\mathbb{R}^N$ gauge theory. We implement this condensation microscopically by gauging a non-on-site 1-form symmetry of the $\mathbb{R}^N$ toric code.
authors: Marvin Qi, Wilbur Shirley

papers.title: Gauge and scale dependence of the quadratic backreaction source during inflation: Uniform-expansion gauge
papers.abstract: Cosmological backreaction is most directly expressed through the local expansion of the spacetime foliation, so uniform-expansion (UE) slicing provides a natural geometrical setting in which to examine the quadratic effective energy-momentum tensor (2EMT) of scalar perturbations during slow-roll inflation. We impose the complete scalar gauge conditions $\kappa=0$ and $E=0$. The uniform-expansion condition gives a \textit{differential} constraint for the shift $Q$ in configuration space and satisfies $Q_{\mathrm{UE}}(k)=-3(\Psi'+\mathcal H\Psi)/(k^2+3\epsilon\mathcal H^2)$ for each Fourier mode. In the strict infrared, the UE source vanishes at zero gradient, while its first nonzero terms are $\widehat\tau_{00}^{\mathrm{UE}}/\mathcal F_{\mathrm{LW}} \simeq8\sigma_1^2/\epsilon$ and $\widehat\tau_{ii}^{\mathrm{UE}}/\mathcal F_{\mathrm{LW}} \simeq-8\sigma_1^2/(3\epsilon)$ at leading slow-roll order. Thus $w_{\rm raw}^{\mathrm{UE}}\simeq-1/3$, but the first finite-gradient coefficients differ from the comoving and uniform-density gauges. Sufficiently deep in the gradient-dominated intermediate infrared, the leading UE behavior approaches the spatially-flat result, whereas the crossover region between the strict and intermediate infrared regimes requires the full expressions for the 2EMT. In the ultraviolet, we have $\widehat\tau_{00}^{\mathrm{UE}}\simeq2\mathcal F_{\mathrm{SW}}$ and $\widehat\tau_{ii}^{\mathrm{UE}}\simeq(2/3)\mathcal F_{\mathrm{SW}}$, yielding $w_{\mathrm{raw}}\simeq1/3$. Separately, we demonstrate the gauge dependence of the 2EMT under general scalar gauge transformations and discuss the complete fixing of the UE gauge.
authors: Inyong Cho

papers.title: Quantum Parallel Algorithm for Multivariate Trace Estimation with Applications
papers.abstract: Estimating multivariate traces Tr(A1A2......Ak) is a fundamental task arising across diverse fields. In this paper, We develop a quantum algorithm for this problem tailored to near-term quantum devices. We access matrices by preparing their vectorized states. This access mode yields a tensor-network representation of the multivariate trace, which in turn guides the design of a parallel algorithm. The resulting circuit has depth dominated solely by that of the input oracle and independent of the number of matrices k, at the cost of a qubit count scaling as {\Theta}(k)-a trade-off between circuit depth and circuit size. Moreover, the circuit exhibits a simple modular structure that allows explicit distribution over O(k) devices. We further establish efficient preparation circuits for a broad range of matrix classes, demonstrating the wide applicability of our approach. we present two applications: spectral sum estimation and a quantum implementation of the classical Lanczos method. Both reduce the target problem to sums of multivariate traces, thereby avoiding the construction of matrix polynomial transformations and achieving two levels of parallelism. For certain matrix classes, the resulting algorithms reduce circuit depth by a factor equal to the degree of the approximating polynomial. The shallow circuit depth and distributed implementation make our algorithms particularly suitable for near-term devices.
authors: Honghong Lin, Yun Shang

papers.title: Holomorphic Feynman diagrams in four dimensions and the quantum BPS ring
papers.abstract: We compute, at all loop orders, the kernels of the holomorphic Feynman graphs that carry the loop corrections to supersymmetry transformations and to regularized products of local operators in the holomorphic twist of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=1$ supersymmetric gauge theories. The current equations of these holomorphic graph integrals are those of an electrical network. Schwinger parameters are resistances and holomorphic momenta are injected currents. Iterating series, parallel and star--triangle reductions on Schwinger space gives the fan, spider and cubic product-forest kernels at all loop orders. Assuming that twisting commutes with quantization for these composite operators, we identify the twisted differential with their loop-corrected supersymmetry transformation. We give every perturbative correction to the supersymmetry transformation in $\mathcal N=4$ Yang--Mills theory, including its action on operators with arbitrary holomorphic derivatives. Using the marked higher operations of Gaiotto, Kulp and Wu, we also construct and compute the quantum product of operators and prove that, on $\mathbf Q$-cohomology, it is associative, graded commutative and unital, supplying the multiplication of the quantum BPS ring. Every multi-graviton operator thus has an explicit finite completion to a cocycle of the full quantum supercharge. Our computer census finds new fortuitous classes and one-loop lifts in $\mathcal N=4$ Yang--Mills theory with several gauge groups. We have found no two-loop lift in the sectors tested. We also find two-loop lifts in the Leigh--Strassler and $\beta$-deformations of $\mathcal N=4$ Yang--Mills theory. In other theories, we find two-, three- and four-loop lifts in abelian gauge theories, and two- and three-loop lifts in $\mathcal N=2$ $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$ gauge theories and their singlet deformations.
authors: Botao Li, Kangning Liu, Chi-Ming Chang

papers.title: Gradient Blindness in Adaptive Architecture Search for IQP Born Machines
papers.abstract: Instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) Born machines learn a probability distribution from data with a circuit of commuting gates that a classical computer trains at hundreds of qubits. Adaptive algorithms grow a sparse circuit from a small seed by adding in every round the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient. Such algorithms never add a candidate whose gradient vanishes, so the choice of seed decides which circuits they can reach. Here we show that a candidate gate has a nonzero gradient for some angles of the circuit exactly when its generator is the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already in the circuit. The common seed of one-qubit gates therefore never adds a gate on an even number of qubits, which exact gradients on 12 qubits confirm. A seed of one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree sees every candidate, and its circuits match the full circuits on 12 and 16 qubits with 10 to 13 percent of their parameters. At 484 qubits, a heredity pool keeps the search over higher-order gates feasible, and the circuits grown from this seed reach a lower test loss than the dense two-body circuit with 6 percent of its parameters, although the higher-order gates add no gain.
authors: Sebastian W\"olckert, Gerhard Stenzel, Michael Poppel, Claudia Linnhoff-Popien, Jonas Stein

papers.title: A relativistic gravitisation of quantum theory?
papers.abstract: We develop a model, that we call local semiclassical gravity, based on the distributional semiclassical Einstein field equations (EFEs) sourced by the local quantum state, i.e. the reduced density matrix of the local system updated by collapses (only) in its past light cone. We propose this as the basis of a relativistically causal generally covariant gravitisation of relativistic quantum theory in $1+3$ spacetime dimensions. We derive the weak-field limit which exhibits the explicitly causal dynamical structure of the theory, and recover the Schr\"odinger-Newton (SN) system in the nonrelativistic limit. This proposal can thus be understood as a causal completion of the SN equation, a nonlinear extension to quantum theory. We analyze relativistic quantum measurements in this nonlinear setup, showing that these do not lead to superluminal signalling if quantum states update (only) in the future light-cone of the measurement region. We give explicit examples of quantum measurements on a spatial superposition and on entangled subsystems showing how, in the weak field limit, discontinuities in the expectation value of the stress-energy tensor can be consistent with distributional solutions to the (linearised) semiclassical EFEs. We also highlight that the theory allows non-standard measurements via its nonlinearities. These effective ``readout devices'' can approximately determine a quantum state without affecting it through the state's influence on the classical gravitational field and hence can implement approximate quantum state cloning. Nonetheless, the theory does not allow superluminal signalling, although it does violate the quantum no-signalling principle. We further show that the classical gravitational field is generally not locally causal in the sense of Bell. We present several paths to test the model against low-energy quantum gravity in tabletop experiments.
authors: Samuel Fedida, Adrian Kent

papers.title: Grade Restriction Rule For D-Brane Transport In Non-Abelian Gauged Linear Sigma Models
papers.abstract: We study the low energy behaviour of B-type D-branes in non-Abelian gauged linear sigma models. The main problem is to determine the grade restriction rule for D-brane transport from one phase to another along paths. We analyze the convergence condition of the integral for the hemisphere partition function. We perform a thorough analysis in a particular model with two phases, one weakly coupled and one strongly coupled, both corresponding to Calabi-Yau threefolds. General methods are developed in this study and are applied to other models successfully. The integrals for a set of special Chan-Paton representations exhibit critical behaviour around each singular point on the phase boundary. From each of these points emanate ``no entry zones'' where a convergent contour is lost or is forced to traverse Gamma function poles. Knowledge of the special representations and no entry zones is strong enough to uniquely determine the grade restriction rule. In the course of this study, we encounter a problem in Weyl invariance of convergent contours, which forces us to modify the grade restriction criterion. The special representations play an important r\^ole in the monodromy around the singular point. We also obtain exact results on boundary conditions in supersymmetric QCDs and apply them to understand the low energy behaviour of D-branes in the strong coupling phase.
authors: Richard Eager, Kentaro Hori, Johanna Knapp, Mauricio Romo

papers.title: Neither graphs nor hypergraphs: structural moments of higher-order interactions determine stochastic social-impact dynamics
papers.abstract: Whether higher-order interactions can be reduced to simpler representations is a question about the dynamics they drive, not only about their structure: what can be discarded is whatever the dynamics does not see. We make this precise for binary-state stochastic dynamics in which each agent, when updated, interacts with a randomly selected group and changes state according to the fraction of disagreeing members, as in generalized voter and social-impact models on hypergraphs. We ask which statistics of the group-interaction process determine the resulting Markov dynamics. For response functions that are polynomials of degree $q$, the answer is a hierarchy of size-weighted inclusion moments, which we call structural moments, involving at most $q$ neighbors at a time, regardless of how large the groups are. These moments are not only sufficient but also necessary: two interaction structures produce identical dynamics for all such rules if and only if their moments coincide. More generally, each class of rules selects its own minimal structural description, ranging from weighted pairwise links for linear rules to the full distribution of co-membership by group size for arbitrary rules. For voter-type rules, the same moments also reconstruct exact pairwise copying representations of these dynamics.
authors: Emanuele Cozzo

papers.title: In-memory measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution
papers.abstract: Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.
authors: Nicolas Gauriot, Samuel Morrissey, Paul M. Burdekin, Ilse Maillette de Buy Wenniger, Sarah E. Thomas, Ian A. Walmsley, Robert I. Woodward, R. Mark Stevenson

papers.title: Amplifying or Redistributing Coupling: Synchronization in Sparse Adaptive Oscillator Networks
papers.abstract: Synchronization -- different units falling into a common rhythm -- matters in systems ranging from electrical generators to populations of neurons. But what happens when the connections that coordinate their timing can also change? If two units become more closely aligned and their connection strengthens, that extra influence can either increase the total coupling received by a unit or take a larger share of a fixed total. We examine these alternatives in a mathematical network of oscillators, each representing a repeating cycle, connected by sparse directed links. We compare constant connections with two adaptive rules that favor phase-aligned neighbors: unconstrained Hebbian coupling and homeostatic normalization, which keeps the total incoming effective coupling of each oscillator constant. Exact relationships establish this conservation and show that the mean Hebbian weight relaxes toward a value set by alignment along the network links. In matched numerical experiments, unconstrained adaptation reaches a given level of collective synchrony at weaker imposed coupling than fixed connections, whereas the normalized network requires stronger coupling within the same observation window. Longer observations reveal distinct individual trajectories, including increasing, sustained, and declining coherence. The central lesson is that the collective consequences of adaptation depend not only on which links are strengthened, but also on whether their strengthening adds influence or redistributes it.
authors: Yousef Jamali (Complex Systems Laboratory, Department of Applied Mathematics, School of Mathematical Sciences, Tarbiat Modares University, Tehran, Iran)

papers.title: Asymptotic analysis of a $3\times3$-doubly periodic random lozenge tiling model of a hexagon
papers.abstract: We study a random lozenge tiling model of a regular hexagon with weights that are doubly periodic with period $3$. This model features a smooth phase with six cusp points. We obtain explicit descriptions of the limit shape and the local scaling limits of the correlation kernel. Both limits are expressed as contour integrals on the Harnack curve that underlies the model, or on its double cover that is obtained by gluing together two copies along the support of an equilibrium measure in an external field. Our asymptotic analysis is based on the double contour integral representation of the correlation kernel due to Duits and Kuijlaars. This double contour integral contains a factor that is given in terms of the solution of a Riemann-Hilbert problem for matrix-valued orthogonal polynomials. The asymptotic behavior of this Riemann-Hilbert problem was recently studied by one of the authors using the Deift-Zhou method of steepest descent. In this work, we complement this approach with the asymptotic analysis of the double contour integral. The integrals are moved to the double cover of the Harnack curve. We analyze the effect of the first two transformations of the Deift-Zhou method, and deform the contours to the relevant saddle points. We visualize our asymptotic analysis on the amoeba of the Harnack curve, in the spirit of the work of Berggren and Borodin on the doubly periodic Aztec diamond.
authors: Max J. van Horssen, Arno B. J. Kuijlaars

papers.title: A characterization of uniformly discrete crystalline measures with unit weights
papers.abstract: We prove that every uniformly discrete set $\emptyset\ne\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ admitting a Fourier summation formula with a discrete set of frequencies $S(\Lambda)\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ arises from the Alon--Kummer--Kurasov--Vinzant construction using a Lee--Yang variety. In particular, every crystalline measure with uniformly discrete support and unit weights is a Fourier quasicrystal coming from the above construction. It also implies that every set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d\subset\mathbb{C}^d$ as above is the common zero set in $\mathbb{C}^d$ of finitely many trigonometric polynomials, extending the one-dimensional theorem of Olevskii and Ulanovskii. As part of the proof, we generalize Meyer's notion of lighthouse measures to higher codimension and introduce lighthouse manifolds, which we characterize, up to a monomial change of coordinates, as the torus parts of Lee--Yang varieties.
authors: Lior Alon, Mario Kummer

papers.title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.
authors: Eduardo Reck Miranda, Moein Fahmideh Vatandoost

papers.title: Semiclassical Quantum Mechanics and the Optics of Time-Varying Media
papers.abstract: Rapid, high contrast modulation of optical parameters such as the refractive index can radically reshape a wave's frequency spectrum as it propagates. Non-commuting frequency and time operators can be used to describe this reshaping, analogous to the position and momentum operators of quantum mechanics. Here we develop the connection between this theory and semi-classical quantum mechanics, showing that: (i) different microscopic models of time-varying materials are equivalent to choices of operator ordering; (ii) wave propagation is governed by an unusual non-Hermitian Schr\"odinger equation; (iii) we can take a semi-classical limit, finding a generalization of Hamilton's equations governing the central frequency and arrival time of a wave spectrum as it propagates through a modulated material. The theory can be applied to design dispersive time modulations that `focus' a wave in frequency and time, analogous to caustics in semiclassical quantum mechanics. Our results not only deepen the connection between classical wave propagation and quantum mechanics, but can also simplify overly complex calculations that have been previously applied to media where time reflection effects are negligible.
authors: S. A. R. Horsley, R. Sokol, E. -M. Graefe

papers.title: Quantifying extractable imaginarity with qubit triangles
papers.abstract: Two qubit states with the same robustness of imaginarity can differ in the robustness attainable by real filtering on a successful outcome. We represent the input robustness $R$ and the largest conditional robustness $\kappa$ by the base of a right triangle and the slope of its hypotenuse, respectively. Twice the area, $R^2\kappa$, defines a faithful, convex measure that is monotone on average under real instruments. In arbitrary finite dimensions, maximizing the mean normalized area of the extracted qubits gives the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension of the qubit measure. We derive computable bounds on this area by determining the maximum mean squared robustness of the output qubits. This maximum equals the Bures quantum $\chi^2$ divergence between the input and its real part. A projection onto orthogonal real subspaces attains the maximum and, when its outcome is retained, preserves the quantum Fisher information at the midpoint of a mixture of the input and its complex conjugate. We obtain exact areas for states with commuting real and imaginary parts and for pure states mixed with white noise. Two eight-dimensional states have identical $R$, $\kappa$, and optimal mean squared robustness, yet their different areas rule out deterministic conversion by real operations in one direction.
authors: Meng-Li Guo, Chen-Xin Xu, Wen Xu, Shao-Ming Fei

papers.title: A Convex-Roof Affinity-Square Measure of Quantum Imaginarity
papers.abstract: Quantum imaginarity characterizes the part of a quantum state that cannot be represented by real density matrices in a fixed reference basis. We study an affinity-square measure of imaginarity for pure states and its convex-roof extension to mixed states. The pure state quantity is defined by minimizing the affinity-square measure over the convex set of real states. This optimization admits a closed expression determined by the modulus of the conjugation overlap between a state and its complex conjugate. The measure vanishes precisely when the state is real up to a global phase. We prove that the convex-roof extension is faithful, convex, monotone under real operations, and nonincreasing on average under selective real operations. For arbitrary single-qubit mixed states, we evaluate the convex roof exactly and express it in terms of the imaginary component of the off-diagonal density-matrix element. We also compare pure-state imaginarity with an auxiliary affinity-square coherence functional and give the corresponding phase weights.
authors: Nan-Nan Guan, Meng-Li Guo, Xue-Na Zhu, Zhi-Xiang Jin, Yan-Hui Zhou

papers.title: Phase transitions in work fluctuations in correlated N-particle resets
papers.abstract: Systems of $N$ independent uncorrelated particles subjected to the same stochastic change in the environment have recently been studied both theoretically and in experiments, to elucidate the interesting phenomenon of dynamically emergent interparticle positional correlations. However, the thermodynamic cost of creating such correlations, as well as its interplay with the initial distribution of the $N$ particles has not been studied. In this paper, we study systems of $N$ particles that are simultaneously subjected to a switch of an external potential, either stochastically or periodically, beginning from arbitrarily correlated initial states. We map out the distribution of thermodynamic work for such a system in the full parameter space of the problem that includes the number of particles $N$, arbitrary initial correlations between particles and arbitrary initial reduced single particle distributions.
